attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the image bubble from each [set sprite to] block into a bubble in the [set list to] array block?
steps.senseiHelp:
❓ Did you drag the image bubble from each [set sprite to] block into a bubble in the [set list to] array block?

❓Which button can be used to add a third bubble to the array inside the [set list to] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Explain to the Ninja that an array stores items in an ordered list. Variables store individual items, whereas arrays store multiple items of the same type (e.g. strings, numbers, images).
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by creating an array, or list, of farm animals! 


Click Advanced at the bottom of the code block menu, open Arrays, then drag a [set list to] block into the [on start] container, above the [set score to] block. Click + to add a third bubble to the [set list to] block.


Drag the images in the [set sprite to] blocks already in the [on start] container into the [set list to] block. Then, delete each of the three [set sprite to] blocks from the [on start] container.


Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen! The animal images will not appear until an event that will make the sprites appear on the screen is coded.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a (get random value from (list)) value block into the [set sprite to] block in the [on button pressed] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when you press the A button? Which animal image appears?

❓ How else have you used randomness in projects before? 

❓ Why might selecting random values from the array make the project more interesting?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Since arrays store items in an ordered list, it allows you to pull values from a specific place in the list, or in this case, randomly. Explain to the ninja that adding an element of randomness adds an element of surprise to the project.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to make the sprites in the array appear on screen! 


Drag out an [on button pressed] container and place a [set sprite to] block inside. Set the sprite kind to “Animal” in the [set sprite to] block.


Then, open Arrays and drag out a (get random value from (list)) value block. Place it in the sprite image bubble of the [set sprite to] block. 


Click ▶ to see random farm animals appear on the screen when the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the green grass tile in the two [place sprite on top of random tile] blocks, and update the sprite name and sprite kind?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when two animals appear on the same green grass tile?

❓What other types of overlap events might be interesting to add into this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to change both sprite kinds in the [on (Animal) overlaps (Animal)] container and to drag the (otherSprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block.
steps.instructions:
Place the farm animals on random green grass tiles on the tilemap! 


Drag a [place sprite on top of random tile] block into the [on button pressed] container and select the green grass tile. Duplicate this block and drag it into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container.


In the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container, set both sprite kinds to “Animal,” and drag the (otherSprite) bubble into the [place sprite on top of random tile] block. This will prevent 2 different Animal sprites from appearing on the same green grass tile!


Click ▶ to see random farm animals appear on random green grass tiles when the A button is pressed, and change position when overlapping!

steps.hints: ❓ Does your code have three [if then] conditionals that each check if (mySprite image) is equal to image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do you think the <picture is equal to image> comparison block will be useful? What will happen if a certain image appears on the screen?

❓ How is using three [if then] conditionals different than adding an [else] condition?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Using multiple [if then] conditionals can be helpful to check each image individually. With an [if then else], the [else] condition is only executed if the first condition is false.
steps.instructions:
Code the sprites to say something when they appear on the screen!


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on button pressed] container. 


Click Advanced at the bottom of the code block menu, open Images, then drag out a <picture is equal to image> comparison block to replace the <true> section of the [if then] conditional.


Next, open Sprites to use a (mySprite image) bubble as the (picture) in the <picture is equal to image> comparison block.


Duplicate the entire [if then] conditional two times, and add the new blocks into the [on button pressed] container.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you duplicate each image in the [set list to] array, then place one in the image bubble of each <picture is equal to image> comparison block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What sounds do a chicken and a bunny make?

❓ Did you update the message in each [say] block so that the text matches the sound each animal makes?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Using the <picture is equal to image> comparison block will enable the project to determine which sprite image is pulled from the array, and trigger an action to happen without using a variable. In this case, it will check if the specified image is pulled from the array, and share the corresponding message in the [say] block.
steps.instructions:
Continue adding code to make the sprites say something when different animals appear! 


Using the images found in the [set list to] block, duplicate each animal image and place the new version in each of the gray boxes in the <picture is equal to image> comparison blocks.


Drag a [say] block into each conditional and change the message to the sound that animal makes. Click + to update the time parameter for each [say] block too.


Click ▶ and press the A button to see random animals appear on the screen and say the sounds that each animal makes!

steps.hints: ❓ Does the [forever] loop check if (score) is greater than the (length of array)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is being checked in the [if then] conditional in the [forever] loop?

❓ How is the (score) variable being used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The (length of array) block counts the number of items in a list. In this case, the project is constantly checking to see if the score is greater than the number of items in the list, and if so, will show the message, “Too many animals on your farm!”
steps.instructions:
Keep count of how many animals appear on the screen and determine when there are too many! 


Add a [change score by] block at the very top of the [on button pressed] container. 


Then, drag an [if then] conditional into the [forever] loop. Drag out a <0=0> comparison block and place it in the <true> section of the [if then] conditional. Change the comparison to greater than (>) and drag a (score) bubble into the left parameter. 


Open Arrays and drag a (length of array) block into the right parameter of the comparison block. Add a [show long text] block into the [if then] conditional and type, “Too many animals in the pasture!”, into the parameter. 


Click ▶ to see the score increase as more animals appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace the (list) variable with an (array of all tile locations) block, with the green grass tile selected?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does adding an (array of all tile locations) block change what the [if then] conditional checks for? 

❓ What condition needs to be met in order for the message, “Too many animals on your farm!” to be shown and the game to end? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 By adding the (array of all tile locations) block, the [if then] conditional now checks if the score is greater than the number of all green tile locations. If the condition is met, the message is shown and the game ends.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The project isn’t working properly—it only lets 3 animals, which is the number of items in the array, appear on the screen! Change this so animals appear until all of the green grass tiles are covered.


Open Scene and drag an (array of all tile locations) block into the (list) variable of the (length of array) block. Delete the (list) variable as needed and select the green grass tile instead. Then, add a [game over] block set to <LOSE> underneath the [show long text] block in the [if then] conditional. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when there are too many animals on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you click the + on the [set list to] code block to add another animal image to the array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What other animal might you add to the array? What sound does it make?

❓What effects might you add to match the images that appear on the screen?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open-ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project with additional animals in the array! 


Add another animal to the array in the [set list to] block and another condition to make it say the appropriate animal sound in the [on button pressed] container. 


After, customize the project in other ways by adding directions, editing the dialog frame and/or tilemap, and adding screen or sound effects!


Click ▶ to see this finished project in action!

subgroups.introduction: Build a project that uses arrays to randomly place animals on the farm!

validationItems.text: Use an array to contain the different animal images.
Select an animal from the array when the A button is pressed.
Place animals on a random green tile, moving to a different tile if there is already an animal on that tile.
Have the animal say something when placed, based on its image.
Use the score variable to track the number of animals on the grass.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about user input, variables, and arrays. A variable stores one piece of information, while an array stores multiple pieces of information, of the same data type, in an ordered list. Variables and arrays can take in information while they are being created, while the program is running, and from user input. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Save the Data
badges.description: Create variables and arrays to store and use data in a project.

badges.title: Results May Vary
badges.description: Create a new variable and assign it a value.

badges.title: Making a List
badges.description: Create and add items to an array.

badges.title: Dictionary
badges.description: Create and use an array of strings.

badges.title: Art Critic
badges.description: Compare two images to make something happen in a project.
